hints: Think about what bandwidth tells you about frequency - what would it mean if an amplifier worked just as well for very low and very high frequency signals?
walkthrough:
**What bandwidth means**
Think of bandwidth as the range of frequencies that the op-amp can amplify properly. A real op-amp loses gain at high frequencies, so its output gets smaller.

**Ideal case**
For an ideal op-amp this range is infinite, so $$\text{gain is constant for all frequencies}$$ from zero up to infinitely high frequency. There is no cut-off.
Final answer: Infinite bandwidth means the voltage gain is the same for all frequencies of input signal.

hints: Focus on the word rate - it is about how fast the output voltage can change in time when the input changes suddenly.
walkthrough:
**What slew rate measures**
Slew rate is the maximum rate of change of output voltage, $$\text{slew rate} = \left(\frac{dV_{OUT}}{dt}\right)_{max}$$ in $\text{V s}^{-1}$. A real op-amp takes a short time to swing from one voltage to another.

**Ideal case**
Infinite slew rate means there is no limit - the output follows any change in input immediately and exactly, even for a step or very high frequency signal.
Final answer: Infinite slew rate means the output voltage can change instantaneously, with no time delay or distortion.

hints: Look at Fig. 8.1 as a comparator - at the switching point where $V_{OUT}$ is zero, what must be true about the potentials at the - and + inputs?
walkthrough:
**Switching condition for a comparator**
You have an open-loop comparator. $V_{OUT}$ changes sign when $V_-$ crosses $V_+$. So $V_{OUT} = 0$ when $$V_- = V_+$$

**Find the fixed reference $V_+$**
The + input is from a fixed divider across $+4\text{ V}$ to earth: $$V_+ = 4 \times \frac{1.2}{1.8+1.2} = 4 \times \frac{1.2}{3.0} = 1.6\text{ V}$$

**Set $V_-$ equal to this**
The - input is from the thermistor divider: $$V_- = 4 \times \frac{800}{R_T + 800}$$ Set equal to $1.6\text{ V}$: $$1.6 = 4 \times \frac{800}{R_T+800}$$ $$R_T + 800 = \frac{3200}{1.6} = 2000$$ $$R_T = 1200\,\Omega$$

hints: Work out what happens to $V_-$ when $R_T$ gets larger or smaller - remember the $800\,\Omega$ resistor is at the bottom of that divider.
Remember an ideal comparator saturates near its supplies - what are the two possible values of $V_{OUT}$, and at which value of resistance does it flip?
walkthrough:
**Link resistance to $V_-$**
$$V_- = 4 \times \frac{800}{R_T+800}$$ If $R_T$ is large, the denominator is large so $V_-$ is small. If $R_T$ is small, $V_-$ is large. $V_+$ stays fixed at $1.6\text{ V}$.

**Decide saturation**
For $R > R_T$, $V_- < V_+$, so $V_+ > V_-$ and the op-amp saturates positive: $$V_{OUT} \approx +9\text{ V}$$ For $R < R_T$, $V_- > V_+$, so the op-amp saturates negative: $$V_{OUT} \approx -9\text{ V}$$

**Sketch the shape**
As temperature rises, resistance falls from $1.5R_T$ to $0.5R_T$. So start on the right at $+9\text{ V}$, stay flat, then at $R_T$ drop vertically straight down to $-9\text{ V}$, then stay flat to the left. This is the classic comparator switching characteristic.

Final answer: Horizontal line at $V_{OUT} = +9\text{ V}$ for resistance $> R_T$ up to $1.5R_T$, sharp vertical drop at $R_T$ to $V_{OUT} = -9\text{ V}$, then horizontal line at $-9\text{ V}$ down to $0.5R_T$.

hints: From (b)(ii), decide whether $V_{OUT}$ is positive or negative when the thermistor resistance is less than $R_T$ - this is when the LED must be on.
Think about which way conventional current must flow through an LED to light it, and whether current should flow from earth to $V_{OUT}$ or from $V_{OUT}$ to earth in this case.
walkthrough:
**When must the LED be on?**
When $R < R_T$, you found $V_- > V_+$ so $$V_{OUT} = -9\text{ V}$$ Earth is at $0\text{ V}$, which is higher than $-9\text{ V}$. So conventional current can flow from earth down to $V_{OUT}$.

**Orient the LED correctly**
An LED conducts and emits light only in forward direction, from anode (triangle) to cathode (bar). To allow earth to $V_{OUT}$ flow, place the anode towards earth and the cathode towards $V_{OUT}$. Draw the LED symbol on Fig. 8.1 bridging the $V_{OUT}$ line to the earthed common line.

**Check the off state**
When $R > R_T$, $V_{OUT} = +9\text{ V}$, the LED is reverse biased (both ends positive, $V_{OUT}$ higher than earth) so no current flows and it stays off. That gives light only for hot thermistor, $R < R_T$.

Final answer: Connect LED between $V_{OUT}$ terminal and earth (0 V) rail. Orient with anode to earth and cathode to $V_{OUT}$ so it is forward biased when $V_{OUT}$ is negative (-9 V), i.e. when $R < R_T$.
